entities.evidence: The animals go to Noah at the ark, identifying Lamech’s son in the flood account.
God had commanded this same Noah to bring the animals into the ark (Genesis 6:19).

analysis.evidence: The repeated numeral in שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם בָּאוּ describes how the animals came to Noah. זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה identifies the members of each pair as male and female.
analysis.morphology: Masculine dual absolute cardinal numeral, first of two occurrences in a distributive repetition.

analysis.evidence: The marked שְׁנַיִם is the second numeral in שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם. The repetition describes how the animals came to Noah, and זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה identifies the members of each pair as male and female.
analysis.morphology: Masculine dual absolute cardinal numeral, repeated distributively.

analysis.evidence: שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם describes how the animals came, two by two. אֶל נֹחַ names the person they came to, and אֶל הַתֵּבָה identifies the ark as their destination.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person common plural

analysis.evidence: In בָּאוּ אֶל נֹחַ, “they came to Noah,” בָּאוּ expresses motion and the marked אֶל identifies Noah as the person the animals approached.
analysis.morphology: Simple preposition without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for נֹחַ linked to the root article nuach.
draft.definition: Noah, the son whom Lamech names in hope of relief from toil.
draft.evidence: Genesis 5:29 gives the name נֹחַ and explains it through the wordplay on יְנַחֲמֵנוּ, “he will comfort us.”

analysis.evidence: In בָּאוּ אֶל נֹחַ, “they came to Noah,” the marked name is the object of אֶל and identifies the person the animals approached in pairs.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: The pairs came (בָּאוּ) to Noah (אֶל נֹחַ). The second אֶל introduces הַתֵּבָה, the ark they entered.
analysis.morphology: Preposition with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add תֵּבָה under its own consonants תבה. The supplied gentilic gloss and root תאר do not account for the marked noun.
draft.definition: A container that holds living occupants on water, here the ark that carried Noah, his household, and the animals.
draft.evidence: Genesis 7:9 describes the animals entering the ark in pairs. Genesis 7:17–18 describes the floodwaters lifting that same ark until it floated.

analysis.evidence: The two phrases after בָּאוּ identify whom the animals came to and where they went. They came אֶל נֹחַ, “to Noah,” and אֶל הַתֵּבָה, “into the ark.” The article identifies the vessel Noah had already been told to enter with his household in Genesis 7:1.
analysis.morphology: Definite article הַ־ prefixed to a feminine singular absolute common noun.
analysis.sense: The vessel that carried Noah, his household, and the animals through the flood.

analysis.evidence: זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה identifies the animals that entered the ark two by two as male and female. זָכָר designates the male of each pair.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular absolute, used substantivally, with no prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Include the animal use alongside the human use under a single sense of נְקֵבָה.
draft.definition: A female, whether human or animal.
draft.evidence: Genesis 6:19 pairs נְקֵבָה with זָכָר for the animals entering the ark. Genesis 1:27 uses the same pair for humankind.

analysis.evidence: The animals come to Noah שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם, “two by two.” The phrase זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה, “male and female,” identifies the members of each pair.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וּ־ prefixed to a feminine singular absolute common noun.
analysis.sense: The female of an animal pair.

analysis.evidence: כַּאֲשֶׁר introduces צִוָּה אֱלֹהִים אֶת־נֹחַ, “God commanded Noah.” The animals came to the ark in pairs, male and female, just as God had commanded.
analysis.morphology: Relative particle with prefixed comparative preposition כַּ־.
analysis.sense: with a preposition: as, where, than, until

analysis.evidence: In כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֱלֹהִים אֶת נֹחַ, אֱלֹהִים is the subject and אֶת marks Noah as the person God had commanded. כַּאֲשֶׁר connects the animals’ arrival in pairs with that earlier command.
analysis.morphology: Piel perfect, third person masculine singular

analysis.evidence: In כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֱלֹהִים אֶת נֹחַ, “as God commanded Noah,” אֱלֹהִים is the subject of the masculine singular verb צִוָּה. The object marker אֶת identifies Noah as the one God commanded.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine plural absolute, with singular agreement.

analysis.evidence: In צִוָּה אֱלֹהִים אֶת נֹחַ, “God commanded Noah,” אֱלֹהִים is the subject of צִוָּה, and אֶת marks the proper name נֹחַ as its direct object.
analysis.morphology: Unsuffixed direct-object particle, with no prefix

analysis.evidence: In כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה אֱלֹהִים אֶת נֹחַ, “as God commanded Noah,” אֶת marks the final נֹחַ as the person God commanded.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, without prefix or suffix.
